issues.body:
dashboard-gen.py's #1085 rows pin the keepalive mesh as exactly three sources, and this suite already extracts all three real step bodies (`metrics_keepalive_script`, `metrics_specs` at ~line 5194). This PR adds #1375 coverage for `dashboard.yml/registry-keepalive` and `dashboard.yml/sparq-keepalive-dispatch` and none for `metrics.yml/dashboard-publish`.

That third leg (.github/workflows/metrics.yml:287 `for spec in dashboard.yml:1500`, anchor at :301-302) is unchanged and still runs:

    last=$(gh api ".../workflows/${wf}/runs?per_page=1" --jq '.workflow_runs[0].created_at // empty' || true)

So it is the exact pre-#1375 shape, on the highest-consequence target in the estate. scripts/ci-latency-alert.py's M4 comment states the case directly: a rejected workflow KEEPS PRODUCING RUNS with fresh `created_at`, `cron-keepalive` is named as one of the watchers blind to it, and the recorded incidents are an 18-hour dispatcher outage (#1313 -> #1320) and a ~90-minute outage of dashboard.yml (c67c7cdf6 -> #1352) — dashboard.yml being "the HOST of `cron-keepalive` and therefore of the revival mesh for every other scheduled lane".

Net effect of merging as-is: if dashboard.yml is refused at ingestion, its rejected runs still read as fresh to metrics.yml's leg, which stays silent — no kick and, unlike the two legs fixed here, no `::error::` annotation either. The mesh is half-blind in precisely the position where blindness is most expensive.

(Filed against dashboard-gen.py because the mesh contract and the #1375 rows live here and `file` must be a diff path; the code edit itself is in .github/workflows/metrics.yml.)
issues.fix_hint: Apply the same two changes to .github/workflows/metrics.yml:301-302 — widen to `runs?per_page=30`, filter `[.workflow_runs[] | select(.conclusion != "action_required")] | .[0].created_at // empty`, and emit the matching `::error::` when `$last` is empty. Then add the mirrored self-test rows next to the two added here, driving `metrics_keepalive_script`/`metrics_specs` through `run_keepalive_leg` with `runs={"dashboard.yml": [_ka_run(60, conclusion="action_required"), _ka_run(9_999)]}` and with a pure-rejected stream. If the maintainer prefers to keep this PR scoped to #1375's stated target, say so explicitly in the #1085 mesh comment ("leg 3 is knowingly still run-anchored, tracked in #NNNN") so the gap is documented rather than silent — an undocumented half-fix is what this file's own conventions exist to prevent.
issues.title: The defect is fixed on two of the mesh's three legs — metrics.yml/dashboard-publish, the leg watching the mesh HOST, still reads rejected runs as liveness

issues.body:
scripts/ci-latency-alert.py:307-311 is explicit about the false positive: "a scheduled run held by an ENVIRONMENT protection rule can also conclude `action_required` — and this repo does gate privileged jobs on the `dispatch-secrets` environment. That run HAS jobs. Zero jobs is what separates 'GitHub refused to ingest the file' from 'a human has not approved a deployment'." M4 therefore confirms `jobs.total_count == 0` before alarming.

This diff drops every `action_required` run on the conclusion alone. And the gating is real on the watched set — `environment: dispatch-secrets` appears in metrics.yml:40,172, curate.yml:23, groom-core.yml:30, conflict-resolver.yml:28, dispatch.yml:1658,2272.

Why this is minor rather than blocking: an approval-pending run carries `status` of `waiting`/`action_required` (not `completed`), so the #559 live-run guard above catches it and `continue`s before this anchor is consulted. The exposure is the narrower window where such a run has settled to `status: completed` with `conclusion: action_required` — there the keepalive would classify a legitimately-gated lane as having no liveness evidence and kick it every 15 minutes.
issues.fix_hint: Either narrow the filter the way M4 does (confirm zero jobs before discarding the run), or — cheaper and probably sufficient — state the divergence in the anchor comment: note that the #559 live-run guard is what covers approval-pending runs here, so the conclusion test alone is safe, and cite ci-latency-alert.py's M4 note so the two readers of the same signal do not silently drift apart.
issues.title: `action_required` is treated as rejection without the job-count confirmation the repo's own M4 doctrine requires to distinguish it from environment-approval gating

issues.body:
The stub's header comment promises: "an argv this stub does not model exits 64, so a reshaped request fails LOUDLY instead of quietly satisfying the rows above." Previously the live-run read and the anchor read were separated structurally (`per_page=30` vs `per_page=1`). Both are now `per_page=30`, and they are told apart by `[[ "${filter}" == *'status != "completed"'* ]]`.

That couples the harness to the exact spelling of a production jq expression. Reshape the live guard to an equivalent form — e.g. `select(.status == "queued" or .status == "in_progress")`, or `select(.status != "completed")` written with different quoting/spacing — and the live read silently falls into the `else` branch and is served `runs-${wf}.json` instead of exiting 64. It does not pass silently (the #559 guard rows would go red, since their fixtures are written to `live-*.json`), so this is a degraded diagnostic rather than a hole; but a red #559 row pointing at the wrong cause is a much worse signal than exit 64.
issues.fix_hint: Make the split exhaustive: match the live shape and the anchor shape explicitly (e.g. anchor on `*'action_required'*`, live on `*'status != "completed"'*`) and fall through to the existing `printf 'gh-stub: unexpected argv' >&2; exit 64` when a `per_page=30` read matches neither. That restores the stub's stated contract without reintroducing a structural difference in the production URLs.
issues.title: gh-stub now disambiguates two identical URLs by a jq-filter substring, weakening its stated "unmodelled argv exits 64 LOUDLY" contract

issues.body:
Once every run in the newest 30 is `action_required`, `last` is empty, `prev=0`, and `age` is ~epoch-seconds — so this leg POSTs a `workflow_dispatch` and emits an `::error::` on every dashboard tick, i.e. ~96 times a day, indefinitely. If the workflow FILE is refused at ingestion, that dispatch is refused too (creating another 1-second `action_required` run), so the kick is non-curative here in a way it is not for the marker-anchored dispatch leg, where the comment explicitly argues the kick IS curative.

This is a deliberate trade — silence was the bug, and the annotation is the visibility #1375 wants — so it is not a blocker. But the doctrine comment still claims run-anchored kicks are curative, and that is now false for this branch, while the self-test asserts the kick happens without recording that it is expected to be futile.
issues.fix_hint: Add a sentence to THE ANCHOR comment stating that on a pure-rejected stream the kick is knowingly non-curative and the `::error::` annotation is the payload, with recovery owned by ci-latency-alert's M4 alarm (which pages a human). Optionally reference that from the `[#1375] a pure rejected-run stream...` self-test row so the row's intent survives a future reader who wonders why the fleet is dispatching a dead workflow every 15 minutes.
issues.title: A truly ingestion-refused workflow now produces an unbounded 15-minute dispatch loop that cannot revive it

issues.body:
Two cosmetic points on the same hunk.

(1) The artifact anchor twelve lines above deliberately computes `[...| .created_at] | max // empty` rather than trusting position. The new run anchor instead takes `.[0]` of the filtered array, which is correct only because the runs API returns newest-first — true today, but an unstated assumption that the neighbouring code pointedly declines to make.

(2) The reflowed comment now reads: "That is a valid proxy only where an accepted run / IMPLIES the workflow did its work, / and dispatch.yml is the one listed workflow where it does not" — the third line is a four-word orphan, leftover wrapping from the edit.
issues.fix_hint: For (1), mirror the marker anchor: `[.workflow_runs[] | select(.conclusion != "action_required") | .created_at] | max // empty` — same result, order-independent, consistent with the code beside it. For (2), rewrap the three comment lines to the file's ~98-column width.
issues.title: `.[0]` relies on API result ordering where the sibling marker anchor uses an explicit `| max`; and the reflowed comment leaves an orphan line

verdict.summary:
The change itself is sound and the new self-test rows are genuinely non-vacuous. Both keepalive run-anchors move from `runs?per_page=1` + `.workflow_runs[0]` to `per_page=30` + `select(.conclusion != "action_required") | .[0]`, so a fresh ingestion-rejected run can no longer mask a stale accepted one; `.[0].created_at // empty` is safe on an empty filtered array (jq indexes null without error), and the empty case falls through to prev=0 -> huge age -> kick, i.e. fail-toward-liveness, consistent with the marker anchor beside it. The two new registry rows and two new cross-repo rows each red if the `select` or the `::error::` echo is deleted (row 1: rejected@60s ahead of accepted@9999s -> unfiltered reads 60s and does NOT kick; row 2: the substring assertion carries the echo), so they are real kills, not decoration. The gh-stub rework correctly re-routes the now-identical URL on the jq filter.

What blocks approval is COMPLETENESS, not correctness. The keepalive mesh has three legs, pinned by equality in dashboard-gen.py's #1085 rows: dashboard.yml/registry-keepalive, dashboard.yml/sparq-keepalive-dispatch, and metrics.yml/dashboard-publish. Two are fixed here; the third (.github/workflows/metrics.yml:301-302) still reads the raw `.workflow_runs[0].created_at` from `per_page=1` — and it is the leg watching dashboard.yml, which this repo's own M4 doctrine (scripts/ci-latency-alert.py) names as the HOST of the revival mesh and records as having suffered a ~90-minute ingestion-rejection outage. Leaving it unfiltered means the one watcher that could make a refused dashboard.yml visible still reads its rejected runs as liveness.

Three smaller items follow: divergence from M4's documented job-count discriminator, a weakened stub-refusal contract, and an ordering assumption the sibling anchor does not make.
